abstract: Agricultural intensification and habitat fragmentation are major drivers of biodiversity loss, yet their effects on ecological interaction networks remain elusive. In plant-pollinator systems, many species disappear with habitat transformation, but network responses remain inconsistent across studies. We hypothesize that this mismatch arises because local observations often overlook the response diversity of the regional species pools. To test this, we compared observed plant-pollinator networks along a land-use gradient with expectations under hypothetical closed-community simulations. Using data from 30 sites in the Donana Protected Area (southern Spain), we found that spatially connected communities maintained a stable network structure despite habitat loss. This stability was driven by pollinator response diversity, leading to marked species turnover across sites. In contrast, simulated closed communities showed reduced buffering capacity and predominantly negative trends in network metrics such as pollinator richness, total visits, and plant link density. Our results indicate that network stability can emerge from spatial connectivity rather than purely local processes.
